name: Browser Use
tagline: Make websites accessible for AI agents — automate any browser task with LLMs
description: Browser Use lets an AI agent control a web browser the same way a human does — it opens pages, clicks buttons, types text, fills forms, and extracts data. You describe the task in natural language and the agent completes it end to end. The library wraps a headless or headed Chromium session behind a clean Python API: you pick your LLM (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, or the project's own optimised model), instantiate an Agent with a task string, and call agent.run(). Under the hood the agent observes the page through an accessibility-tree snapshot, decides an action, executes it via CDP, and loops until the task is done. Real-world use-cases include filling job applications from a resume, extracting structured follower data to CSV, QA-testing a local website for bugs and visual inconsistencies, and any repetitive browser workflow you would otherwise script with Selenium or Playwright. The project ships both an open-source Python library you run locally and a fully-hosted cloud agent with stealth browsing, proxy rotation, captcha solving, and 1000+ integrations. It is the number-one agent on the Odysseys benchmark with 87.4 percent average across 200 long-horizon web tasks, ahead of computer-use agents from OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and Microsoft. The CLI lets coding agents like Claude Code and Codex install a skill and drive the browser directly. With 108 000+ GitHub stars and an MIT licence, it is the most popular open-source browser-automation agent available.

curatorNote: The runaway success of AI browser agents — 108K stars and MIT-licensed. Browser Use proved that giving an LLM an accessibility-tree view of a web page and a simple action loop is enough to automate nearly any browser task. The benchmark results are not just marketing: it tops the independent Odysseys leaderboard ahead of every major lab's computer-use offering.
